screens.title: Dimensional Modeling: Star and Snowflake Schemas
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to structure a data warehouse so analytical queries run fast and make sense to business users. Dimensional modeling separates measurements from descriptive context: facts hold the numbers, and dimensions hold the who, what, where, and when that give those numbers meaning. You will see the two dominant shapes used in analytics — the Star Schema and the Snowflake Schema — and learn when to favor one over the other. We will also cover how to preserve history for changing attributes using Slowly Changing Dimensions. Practically, you will be able to design a Star Schema for e-commerce sales, read a simple S Q L aggregation that joins facts to dimensions, and choose an SCD strategy for customer attributes. A good model balances query speed, storage, and clarity for analysts. To make this concrete, the lesson includes example table DDL for a SalesFact and ProductDimension, a sample aggregation query by year and category, and a hands-on activity to create schema statements for product, customer, and time dimensions. As you move through the slides, notice the trade-offs between redundancy and join complexity, and ask yourself which matters most for your reports and dashboards.

screens.title: What is Dimensional Modeling?
screens.narratorSegment: Dimensional modeling is a logical design approach for data warehouses that focuses on making analytical queries simple and fast. In this approach you separate business measurements, called facts, from descriptive context, called dimensions. Facts are numeric events — like sales quantity, revenue, or transaction count — and each fact row usually contains foreign keys that point to the dimension rows that describe the event. Dimensions contain descriptive attributes like product name, customer segment, or calendar fields and are typically denormalized to make queries simpler. The practical reason for denormalization is fewer joins and clearer queries for analysts and BI tools. A common misconception is that denormalization is sloppy; in analytics it is intentional, because redundancy in dimensions trades storage for query performance and understandability. For example, a SalesFact row might store foreign keys to Product, Customer, Store, and Time dimensions while measures hold QuantitySold and UnitPrice. When you design a dimensional model, list the measures first, then identify the dimensions that provide the necessary filtering and grouping. A quick test is to imagine the typical dashboard questions and ensure the model supports those groupings without many nested joins. Reflect: which business questions must your model answer, and which dimensions are required to make those answers easy?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Dimensional modeling organizes data into facts (measures) and dimensions (descriptors) to optimize analytic queries and usability.

content.html:
Core Concept Definition
Facts and Dimensions
Facts record the numeric events. Dimensions describe those events so you can filter, group, and label aggregates.
Fact Table (example)
SalesFact: OrderID, DateID, ProductID, CustomerID, QuantitySold, UnitPrice, TotalSaleAmount
Dimension Table (example)
ProductDimension: ProductID, ProductName, ProductCategory, ProductBrand
Key Takeaway

Design around the questions analysts need to ask: list measures first, then choose dimensions that enable those groupings efficiently.

Analogy: Facts are the ledger; dimensions are the index
Concrete example
A sales transaction row links to a product row that includes category and brand so you can report revenue by brand without extra joins.
Common mistake
Over-normalizing dimensions because OLTP habits leak into analytics design, causing slow queries and complex reports.
Check your understanding
If you need to frequently group by customer segment and city in reports, include those attributes in CustomerDimension rather than joining to a separate lookup at runtime.

screens.title: Fact Table Anatomy and SQL Example
screens.narratorSegment: A fact table stores the measurements of a business process and the foreign keys that tie those measurements to context. Typical columns include a technical key, foreign keys to dimensions, and numeric measures such as QuantitySold, UnitPrice, and TotalSaleAmount. The fact table is usually narrow and very large, optimized for aggregations. It avoids descriptive columns and relies on dimensions for labels. To make this concrete, consider a SalesFact with keys linking to time, product, customer, and store dimensions. The S Q L DDL declares the primary key and foreign key references. When you write this DDL, pick precise data types for measures and keys so joins and aggregations are efficient. A common misconception is placing descriptive attributes into the fact table; that duplicates data and makes maintenance harder. Instead, keep the fact focused and let dimensions provide text and hierarchical attributes. Below you will see a compact CREATE TABLE example for SalesFact and ProductDimension. Use that pattern as a baseline for your own fact tables, then test aggregations with sample queries to validate cardinality and performance assumptions. A good follow-up question is: which columns will be filtered most often, and how will you index them?

keyIdea.title: Fact design principle
keyIdea.text: Keep facts narrow and numeric, use keys to join to descriptive dimensions, and choose types suitable for aggregation.

content.html:
Definition Fact Table Anatomy
SalesFact (structure)
Technical key, foreign keys to dimensions, and measures. No long text fields here.
-- Fact Table
CREATE TABLE SalesFact (
  SalesFactID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  DateID INT NOT NULL,
  ProductID INT NOT NULL,
  CustomerID INT NOT NULL,
  StoreID INT NOT NULL,
  QuantitySold INT NOT NULL,
  UnitPrice DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  TotalSaleAmount DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (DateID) REFERENCES TimeDimension(DateID),
  FOREIGN KEY (ProductID) REFERENCES ProductDimension(ProductID),
  FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES CustomerDimension(CustomerID),
  FOREIGN KEY (StoreID) REFERENCES StoreDimension(StoreID)
);
ProductDimension (example)
Dimension tables hold descriptive attributes and are often denormalized to reduce joins in queries.
-- Dimension Table: ProductDimension
CREATE TABLE ProductDimension (
  ProductID INT PRIMARY KEY,
  ProductName VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  ProductCategory VARCHAR(100),
  ProductBrand VARCHAR(100),
  ProductColor VARCHAR(50)
);
Example query
Aggregate sales by calendar year and product category using direct joins between fact and dimensions.
SELECT td.CalendarYear,
       pd.ProductCategory,
       SUM(sf.TotalSaleAmount) AS TotalSales
FROM SalesFact sf
JOIN TimeDimension td ON sf.DateID = td.DateID
JOIN ProductDimension pd ON sf.ProductID = pd.ProductID
WHERE td.CalendarYear = 2023
GROUP BY td.CalendarYear, pd.ProductCategory
ORDER BY TotalSales DESC;

screens.title: Star Schema: Structure and Advantages
screens.narratorSegment: The Star Schema places one central fact table at the heart of the model, with denormalized dimension tables radiating outward. Each join from the fact to a dimension is direct and uses a single foreign key, which keeps queries simple and fast. The biggest advantages are straightforward S Q L for analysts, fewer joins in aggregation queries, and easier troubleshooting when results look odd. In practice you design the fact with the measures you need and add dimensions that people will slice and dice on, such as Time, Product, and Customer. A subtle point to notice is redundancy: denormalized dimensions may repeat category or brand names across many product rows. This is acceptable when query speed and ease of use are priorities. A common misconception is that star schemas are always best; sometimes extremely large or highly normalized sources make a Snowflake a better fit. Use the Star shape when storage is reasonable and the reporting workload values simple joins. The takeaway is that Star Schemas trade some duplication for clarity and performance, and they remain the default choice when building business-friendly data marts.

keyIdea.title: Star Schema
keyIdea.text: Star makes querying easy — center facts, denormalize dimensions, and accept controlled redundancy for faster aggregations.

content.html:
Process Flow Star Schema
Star structure
One fact table at center, direct joins to denormalized dimensions for simplicity and speed.
Benefits
  • Fewer joins, faster aggregations
  • Simpler SQL for analysts and BI tools
  • Easy to maintain and understand
Trade-offs
  • Some redundancy in dimensions
  • Potentially larger storage for denormalized text
Analyst tip: Model dimensions to reflect reporting filters and groupings, not the original transactional model.
Visual: E-commerce example (cards)
SalesFact
Keys: DateID, ProductID, CustomerID; Measures: Quantity, Total
ProductDimension
ProductName, Category, Brand
CustomerDimension
Name, Segment, City, State
TimeDimension
FullDate, Day, Month, Quarter, Year
Key Takeaway

Choose Star when you value query simplicity and speed; denormalize dimensions to avoid extra joins in analytics.

screens.title: Snowflake Schema: When and Why
screens.narratorSegment: A Snowflake Schema normalizes dimension tables into sub-dimensions so that hierarchical attributes live in their own tables. For example, ProductDimension might normalize ProductCategory and ProductBrand into separate Category and Brand tables. This reduces redundancy and can improve storage efficiency and data integrity for large, complex dimensions. The downside is extra joins when writing queries: an analyst may need to join SalesFact to ProductDimension and then to CategoryDimension to get the category name. That join complexity can slow queries or complicate BI layers. Choose a Snowflake when dimension attributes themselves are rich, change independently, or when storage and normalization benefits outweigh the need for simple queries. A common misconception is that Snowflake always saves space; normalization helps, but it also requires careful indexing and sometimes ETL complexity. When designing, test representative queries and measure the impact. If you normalize, provide friendly views or materialized layers so analysts see a simpler flattened surface for reporting. In short, Snowflake trades query simplicity for reduced redundancy and potentially better data integrity for large dimensions. Snowflake Schema: When and Why means snowflake reduces redundancy by normalizing dimension attributes, but increases join complexity and can slow analytical queries.. In practical terms, normalize dimensions to reduce redundancy at the cost of extra joins. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Snowflake trade-off
keyIdea.text: Snowflake reduces redundancy by normalizing dimension attributes, but increases join complexity and can slow analytical queries.

content.html:
Comparison Star vs Snowflake
Snowflake structure
Break dimension attributes into logical sub-dimensions to avoid repeating long attribute lists across many rows.
When to use
  • Dimensions are very large or change independently
  • You need strict normalization for data integrity
  • Storage savings outweigh join cost
Caveats
More joins in queries and potential performance hits for ad hoc analytics unless compensated by views or aggregation layers.
Example: Normalize product attributes
ProductDimension
ProductID, ProductName, CategoryID, BrandID
CategoryDimension
CategoryID, CategoryName, Department
BrandDimension
BrandID, BrandName, Manufacturer
Pro tip
If you choose Snowflake, consider offering flattened views or materialized tables that present denormalized attributes for analysts while keeping normalized source tables for storage efficiency.

screens.title: Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD): Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Slowly Changing Dimensions are techniques that determine how a dimension table records changes to descriptive attributes over time. The choice of SCD strategy affects the accuracy of historical analysis. Type 1 simply overwrites the old value with the new one, which is appropriate when historical values are not needed for analysis. Type 2 preserves full history by inserting a new row for the entity with new attribute values while marking the previous row as inactive using StartDate, EndDate, or an IsCurrent flag. This is ideal when you must report using the attribute value that was valid at the time of the fact event. Type 3 keeps a limited history by adding columns for previous values, useful only when you need to track a recent prior state. A common pitfall is choosing Type 1 when historical reporting is required, causing past reports to reflect current attributes and distorting trends. When designing SCDs, ask whether analyses need the attribute value as of the event date. If yes, Type 2 is usually the correct choice. Think about the storage and ETL complexity each approach introduces and how that aligns with reporting requirements.

keyIdea.title: SCD core idea
keyIdea.text: Choose an SCD type based on whether you need to preserve historical attribute values for accurate analysis of past facts.

content.html:
Definition Slowly Changing Dimensions
SCD Type 1
Overwrite attribute. No history preserved. Use when history is not required.
Example: Update customer address in place when historical address is irrelevant.
SCD Type 2
Insert a new row for each change and mark old rows inactive with StartDate, EndDate, IsCurrent. Preserves full history.
Example: Keep past customer addresses to attribute historical orders correctly.
SCD Type 3
Add columns to store limited prior values. Useful for tracking only the most recent previous state.
Example: Keep CurrentEmail and PreviousEmail columns for a brief audit trail.
Common mistake
Using Type 1 when historical reports must show the attribute value at the time of the event, leading to incorrect historical analysis.

screens.title: Implementing SCD Type 1 and Type 2
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing SCDs is an ETL concern as much as a schema design decision. SCD Type 1 is the simplest: the ETL job updates the existing dimension row with new values. This is appropriate for attributes where previous values are irrelevant. Because no history is kept, no extra keys or date columns are required. SCD Type 2 requires the ETL to detect changes to tracked attributes and then insert a new row for the dimension member: the new row represents the new state and the previous row is marked with an EndDate and IsCurrent = false. The new row receives a StartDate, IsCurrent = true, and a new surrogate key. This approach preserves a complete history, letting analysts join facts to the correct dimension row based on the fact's date. A frequent implementation detail is ensuring that joins use the effective date ranges correctly: when joining a fact to a dimension under Type 2, you pick the dimension row whose StartDate ≤ fact. Date and (EndDate is null or fact. Date ≤ EndDate). A common misconception is that Type 2 is always heavier; while it adds rows, it provides the only reliable historical attribution when past values must be preserved. Plan ETL, indexing, and query patterns before committing to an SCD strategy.

keyIdea.title: SCD Implementation
keyIdea.text: Use Type 1 for overwrite when history is irrelevant; use Type 2 to preserve full historical attribute states with StartDate/EndDate and IsCurrent flags.

content.html:
Process Flow SCD Implementation
SCD Type 1 (Overwrite)
ETL updates the existing dimension row. Use when historical attribute state is not needed for analysis.
Example scenario
Customer updates email and business only needs the latest contact for communications; overwrite the email in place.
SCD Type 2 (Add new row)
Insert a new dimension row and set IsCurrent flags or date ranges to preserve history for analysis that must reflect the attribute at event time.
Implementation notes
  • Use surrogate keys for dimension rows
  • Add StartDate, EndDate, and IsCurrent columns
  • Update previous row's EndDate and IsCurrent when inserting a new row
Check your understanding

When a fact needs to reflect the dimension state at event time, prefer Type 2 so historical queries join to the correct dimension row.

screens.title: SCD Type 2: Example Rows and Join Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Type 2 SCD preserves a full history of attribute changes by adding new rows for every change. Conceptually, each dimension member can have multiple rows over time, each with its own surrogate key and validity range. For example, when a customer's address changes, the ETL inserts a new CustomerDimension row with the new address and a new StartDate, sets IsCurrent true, and updates the previous row’s EndDate and IsCurrent false. When analysts run a query to attribute past purchases, the join logic must select the dimension row whose date range covers the fact date: that means choosing the row where StartDate is less than or equal to the fact date and (EndDate is null or fact date is less than or equal to EndDate). This avoids misattributing past transactions to current attributes. A common mistake is forgetting to update the EndDate or relying only on IsCurrent in the dimension without using date ranges in joins, which can break historical attribution if ETL lags occur. Below is a concise example showing two rows for the same customer before and after an address change and the typical join condition used in queries. Reflect: can your reporting queries include fact date conditions to ensure they pick the correct historical row?

Conceptually, each dimension member can have multiple rows over time, each with its own surrogate key and validity range. For example, when a customer's address changes, the ETL inserts a new CustomerDimension row with the new address and a new StartDate, sets IsCurrent true, and updates the previous row’s EndDate and IsCurrent false. When analysts run a query to attribute past purchases, the join logic must select the dimension row whose date range covers the fact date: that means choosing the row where StartDate is less than or equal to the fact date and (EndDate is null or fact date is less than or equal to EndDate). This avoids misattributing past transactions to current attributes. A common mistake is forgetting to update the EndDate or relying only on IsCurrent in the dimension without using date ranges in joins, which can break historical attribution if ETL lags occur. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three core ideas in mind as you design analytic schemas. First, dimensional modeling separates facts and dimensions so measurements are stored independently from descriptive context; this separation improves analyst productivity. Second, a Star Schema centers a fact table and uses denormalized dimensions to deliver fast, simple queries, while a Snowflake normalizes dimensions to reduce redundancy at the cost of more joins. Third, choose an appropriate SCD strategy for dimensional attributes: Type 1 overwrites, Type 2 preserves full history with new rows and date flags, and Type 3 preserves a limited prior state. These decisions determine whether historical reports reflect the attribute values at event time and whether queries remain performant. When in doubt, model for the analyst: list the questions your reports must answer, then design facts, dimensions, and SCD handling to support those questions accurately and efficiently.

What to Remember
Dimensional Modeling

Star vs Snowflake

Summary

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to structure a data warehouse so analytical queries run fast and make sense to business users. Dimensional modeling separates measurements from descriptive context: facts hold the numbers, and dimensions hold the who, what, where, and when that give those numbers meaning. You will see the two dominant shapes used in analytics — the Star Schema and the Snowflake Schema — and learn when to favor one over the other. We will also cover how to preserve history for changing attributes using Slowly Changing Dimensions. Practically, you will be able to design a Star Schema for e-commerce sales, read a simple S Q L aggregation that joins facts to dimensions, and choose an SCD strategy for customer attributes. A good model balances query speed, storage, and clarity for analysts. To make this concrete, the lesson includes example table DDL for a SalesFact and ProductDimension, a sample aggregation query by year and category, and a hands-on activity to create schema statements for product, customer, and time dimensions. As you move through the slides, notice the trade-offs between redundancy and join complexity, and ask yourself which matters most for your reports and dashboards.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to reason about dimensional models and design schemas that support accurate, fast analysis. First, you will learn the core principles of dimensional modeling so you can explain why facts and dimensions are separated and why denormalization is often beneficial for analytics. Second, you will be able to identify and differentiate fact tables and dimension tables in a schema and point to measures and foreign keys that connect them. Third, you will design a Star Schema for an e-commerce example and write the DDL for the central fact table and its dimensions. Finally, you will understand Slowly Changing Dimension strategies and choose between overwrite, add-row, or limited-history approaches depending on whether preserving history is required for analysis. Each objective includes a short rationale and a mnemonic to help you remember when to use each approach.

This second objectives slide focuses on applying the concepts in a practical e-commerce scenario. You will design CREATE TABLE statements for a SalesFact table and three dimensions: Product, Customer, and Time, and ensure appropriate primary and foreign keys. You will also practice choosing data types that fit measures and descriptive fields. Additionally, you will assess when to normalize dimension attributes into sub-dimensions, which leads to a Snowflake Schema, and when to keep them denormalized for performance. Finally, you'll practice deciding which SCD type to use for customer attribute changes, and how to implement the flags and date columns needed for Type 2 history. These tasks bridge theory and real-world modeling decisions for reporting teams and BI tools. More objectives & practical application means design tables with keys and data types, then choose normalization and scd strategies that reflect analysis needs and storage constraints.. In practical terms, skills you'll practice during the hands-on activity. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dimensional modeling is a logical design approach for data warehouses that focuses on making analytical queries simple and fast. In this approach you separate business measurements, called facts, from descriptive context, called dimensions. Facts are numeric events — like sales quantity, revenue, or transaction count — and each fact row usually contains foreign keys that point to the dimension rows that describe the event. Dimensions contain descriptive attributes like product name, customer segment, or calendar fields and are typically denormalized to make queries simpler. The practical reason for denormalization is fewer joins and clearer queries for analysts and BI tools. A common misconception is that denormalization is sloppy; in analytics it is intentional, because redundancy in dimensions trades storage for query performance and understandability. For example, a SalesFact row might store foreign keys to Product, Customer, Store, and Time dimensions while measures hold QuantitySold and UnitPrice. When you design a dimensional model, list the measures first, then identify the dimensions that provide the necessary filtering and grouping. A quick test is to imagine the typical dashboard questions and ensure the model supports those groupings without many nested joins. Reflect: which business questions must your model answer, and which dimensions are required to make those answers easy?

A fact table stores the measurements of a business process and the foreign keys that tie those measurements to context. Typical columns include a technical key, foreign keys to dimensions, and numeric measures such as QuantitySold, UnitPrice, and TotalSaleAmount. The fact table is usually narrow and very large, optimized for aggregations. It avoids descriptive columns and relies on dimensions for labels. To make this concrete, consider a SalesFact with keys linking to time, product, customer, and store dimensions. The S Q L DDL declares the primary key and foreign key references. When you write this DDL, pick precise data types for measures and keys so joins and aggregations are efficient. A common misconception is placing descriptive attributes into the fact table; that duplicates data and makes maintenance harder. Instead, keep the fact focused and let dimensions provide text and hierarchical attributes. Below you will see a compact CREATE TABLE example for SalesFact and ProductDimension. Use that pattern as a baseline for your own fact tables, then test aggregations with sample queries to validate cardinality and performance assumptions. A good follow-up question is: which columns will be filtered most often, and how will you index them?

The Star Schema places one central fact table at the heart of the model, with denormalized dimension tables radiating outward. Each join from the fact to a dimension is direct and uses a single foreign key, which keeps queries simple and fast. The biggest advantages are straightforward S Q L for analysts, fewer joins in aggregation queries, and easier troubleshooting when results look odd. In practice you design the fact with the measures you need and add dimensions that people will slice and dice on, such as Time, Product, and Customer. A subtle point to notice is redundancy: denormalized dimensions may repeat category or brand names across many product rows. This is acceptable when query speed and ease of use are priorities. A common misconception is that star schemas are always best; sometimes extremely large or highly normalized sources make a Snowflake a better fit. Use the Star shape when storage is reasonable and the reporting workload values simple joins. The takeaway is that Star Schemas trade some duplication for clarity and performance, and they remain the default choice when building business-friendly data marts.

A Snowflake Schema normalizes dimension tables into sub-dimensions so that hierarchical attributes live in their own tables. For example, ProductDimension might normalize ProductCategory and ProductBrand into separate Category and Brand tables. This reduces redundancy and can improve storage efficiency and data integrity for large, complex dimensions. The downside is extra joins when writing queries: an analyst may need to join SalesFact to ProductDimension and then to CategoryDimension to get the category name. That join complexity can slow queries or complicate BI layers. Choose a Snowflake when dimension attributes themselves are rich, change independently, or when storage and normalization benefits outweigh the need for simple queries. A common misconception is that Snowflake always saves space; normalization helps, but it also requires careful indexing and sometimes ETL complexity. When designing, test representative queries and measure the impact. If you normalize, provide friendly views or materialized layers so analysts see a simpler flattened surface for reporting. In short, Snowflake trades query simplicity for reduced redundancy and potentially better data integrity for large dimensions. Snowflake Schema: When and Why means snowflake reduces redundancy by normalizing dimension attributes, but increases join complexity and can slow analytical queries.. In practical terms, normalize dimensions to reduce redundancy at the cost of extra joins. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Slowly Changing Dimensions are techniques that determine how a dimension table records changes to descriptive attributes over time. The choice of SCD strategy affects the accuracy of historical analysis. Type 1 simply overwrites the old value with the new one, which is appropriate when historical values are not needed for analysis. Type 2 preserves full history by inserting a new row for the entity with new attribute values while marking the previous row as inactive using StartDate, EndDate, or an IsCurrent flag. This is ideal when you must report using the attribute value that was valid at the time of the fact event. Type 3 keeps a limited history by adding columns for previous values, useful only when you need to track a recent prior state. A common pitfall is choosing Type 1 when historical reporting is required, causing past reports to reflect current attributes and distorting trends. When designing SCDs, ask whether analyses need the attribute value as of the event date. If yes, Type 2 is usually the correct choice. Think about the storage and ETL complexity each approach introduces and how that aligns with reporting requirements.

Implementing SCDs is an ETL concern as much as a schema design decision. SCD Type 1 is the simplest: the ETL job updates the existing dimension row with new values. This is appropriate for attributes where previous values are irrelevant. Because no history is kept, no extra keys or date columns are required. SCD Type 2 requires the ETL to detect changes to tracked attributes and then insert a new row for the dimension member: the new row represents the new state and the previous row is marked with an EndDate and IsCurrent = false. The new row receives a StartDate, IsCurrent = true, and a new surrogate key. This approach preserves a complete history, letting analysts join facts to the correct dimension row based on the fact's date. A frequent implementation detail is ensuring that joins use the effective date ranges correctly: when joining a fact to a dimension under Type 2, you pick the dimension row whose StartDate ≤ fact. Date and (EndDate is null or fact. Date ≤ EndDate). A common misconception is that Type 2 is always heavier; while it adds rows, it provides the only reliable historical attribution when past values must be preserved. Plan ETL, indexing, and query patterns before committing to an SCD strategy.

Type 2 SCD preserves a full history of attribute changes by adding new rows for every change. Conceptually, each dimension member can have multiple rows over time, each with its own surrogate key and validity range. For example, when a customer's address changes, the ETL inserts a new CustomerDimension row with the new address and a new StartDate, sets IsCurrent true, and updates the previous row’s EndDate and IsCurrent false. This avoids misattributing past transactions to current attributes. A common mistake is forgetting to update the EndDate or relying only on IsCurrent in the dimension without using date ranges in joins, which can break historical attribution if ETL lags occur.
